nice maps; but only the truly ignorant would try and ascribe the state-residency data toward something minor, like taxes, when it's obviously clear that the more populated parts of the country are seeing fewer new residents (they're competitive and thus expensive for housing etc) and the areas with space are seeing new people move in. This is all predictable, and GOOD.

Even if something 'minor' like tax differences only impacts 'marginally', for instance a small percentage of the total population, what happens when that marginal impact is skewed heavily toward the 1% everyone wants to tax? Just ask New Jersey.

It doesn't take very many high net worth individuals leaving a state to have a significant impact on tax revenues. Conversely it can be a huge positive benefit to the states where they move their spending and investment.

New Jersey doesn't have a tax problem, it has a municipal and state corruption problem. That's what makes doing business in the state undesirable, not a number on a ledger.

As for the myth that high-net worth individuals flee for tax reasons, that's not actually shown to be true, nor is it a problem. You tax their income in the state, and if they don't make it there well you aren't entitled to taxing it so who cares. There are many arguments on this matter but worldwide it's clear that a narrow range of incomes and wealth is far healthier for the public as a whole.

Certainly wouldn't argue that New Jersey does not have a corruption problem, but that doesn't mean it doesn't have a tax problem as well. Indeed, where do you think they get the money to pay for the corruption?

The nature of income tax varies by state, but the states that I am familiar with tax income 1) if you are a resident and 2) if your income is earned in the state. Indeed, New York state is pretty aggressive in asserting that if you earn anything in New York, then all of your income is New York income -- unless you can demonstrate otherwise. This also creates the unfortunate scenario of individuals who are taxed on their income by multiple states, e.g. Pennsylvania and New York.

Finally, the original article linked presented 'facts'. Of course, facts are subject to interpretation and may be even biased or even incorrect. To be intellectually honest, refute the facts rather than merely asserting they are 'myth'. Would love to see links to studies that successfully repudiate this data. So far I have only found unsubstantiated assertions, which lends credibility to the original link.
